entry: American [[Cable television|cable television]] channel, originally an initialism of Music Television. Launched on August 1, 1981, it first aired [[Music video|music videos]] and related programming hosted by video jockeys (VJs). It later shifted its focus to original [[Reality television|reality]] programming for teenagers and young adults. As of November 2023, it was available to approximately 67 million pay television households in the [[United States]], down from a 2011 peak of 99 million households.

American war comedy-drama television series. Aired on [[CBS]] from September 17, 1972, to February 28, 1983. Developed by Larry Gelbart as a spin-off of the 1970 film of the same name, it follows surgeons and staff at the 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the [[Korean War]] (1950–1953). [[Alan Alda]] played the surgeon Benjamin "Hawkeye" Pierce. The series is usually categorized as a [[Sitcom|situation comedy]], though it has also been described as a "dark comedy" or a "dramedy." Its final episode, "Goodbye, Farewell and Amen," was the most-watched television broadcast in the United States from 1983 to 2010.

Dutch graphic artist who made woodcuts, lithographs, and mezzotints, many inspired by mathematics. His work features impossible objects, explorations of infinity, reflection, [[Symmetry|symmetry]], [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]], polyhedra, hyperbolic geometry, and [[Tessellation|tessellations]]. Although he believed he had no mathematical ability, he interacted with mathematicians including George Pólya and Roger Penrose and researched tessellation himself. In 1922 he visited [[Granada]], Spain, where the tilings of the [[Alhambra]] triggered his interest in the mathematics of tessellation. He was neglected for most of his life and was 70 before a retrospective exhibition was held. His work became widely known among scientists after Martin Gardner featured it in an April 1966 column in *Scientific American*. He was one of the major inspirations for Douglas Hofstadter's Pulitzer Prize–winning 1979 book *Gödel, Escher, Bach*.

American filmmaker and actor known for films with supernatural plots and twist endings. Born in Mahé, India, he was raised in Penn Valley, [[Pennsylvania]]. His breakthrough, *The Sixth Sense* (1999), earned [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay. Later films included *Unbreakable* (2000), *Signs* (2002), and *The Village* (2004), followed by a string of poorly received films before a resurgence with *The Visit* (2015) and *Split* (2016). The cumulative gross of his films exceeds $3.3 billion globally.

Non-orientable surface formed by joining the ends of a strip with a half-twist. Johann Benedict Listing and August Ferdinand Möbius discovered it as a mathematical object in 1858, although it had appeared in Roman mosaics from the third century CE. It has only one side and a single boundary curve. Applications include mechanical belts that wear evenly on both sides, dual-track roller coasters, and world maps printed so that antipodes appear opposite each other. It appears in artworks by [[M. C. Escher]] and in the design of the [[Recycling|recycling]] symbol.

Municipality and capital of Málaga province on the Costa del Sol, [[Andalusia]], Spain (pop., 2025: 597,173). According to most scholars, it was founded about 770 BC by Phoenicians from Tyre. It was under [[Ancient Carthage|Carthaginian]] hegemony from the 6th century BC and under Roman rule from 218 BC. It was placed under Islamic rule in the 8th century, and in 1487 the Crown of Castile gained control. Its economy centers on tourism, construction, technology services, and logistics. It is the 2nd-largest city in Andalusia and the 6th-largest in Spain.

Indigenous [[Polynesia|Polynesian]] people of mainland [[New Zealand]]. Māori descend from East Polynesian settlers who arrived by canoe and developed a distinct culture, whose language and mythology evolved independently of other eastern Polynesian cultures. Early contact with Europeans, starting in the 18th century, ranged from beneficial trade to lethal violence. After the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi, disputed land sales led to conflict in the 1860s and to land confiscations that Māori resisted. Epidemics of introduced disease caused a devastating population decline. The March 2023 census counted 978,246 people of Māori descent, or 19.6% of the total population. Efforts to increase Māori standing have centered on the Treaty of Waitangi, and a cultural revival was bolstered by a protest movement that emerged in the 1960s. Disproportionate numbers of Māori still face economic and social obstacles, including lower life expectancy and incomes.

Capital and largest city of Yucatán state, Mexico (pop., 2020: 921,770). Located slightly inland from the northwest corner of the [[Yucatán Peninsula]], about 35 km (22 mi) from the Gulf of Mexico coast, it is the most populous city on the peninsula and in southeastern Mexico. Its metropolitan area, including Kanasín and Umán, had a population of 1,316,090 in 2020. Spanish conquistadors founded the city in 1542 on the site of the Maya city of Ti'ho, naming it after the town of Mérida in Extremadura, Spain. Its cathedral, built in the late 16th century with stones from nearby Maya ruins, is the oldest cathedral in the mainland [[Americas]]. The city's heritage is a product of [[Syncretism|syncretism]] between Maya and Spanish cultures during the colonial era. In 2022 the UN-Habitat City Prosperity Index recognized it as the city with the highest quality of life in Mexico.

Theoretical framework in [[Physics|physics]] that unifies all consistent versions of [[String theory|superstring theory]]. Edward Witten first conjectured its existence at a string theory conference at the University of Southern California in 1995, starting the second superstring revolution. Before this, string theorists had identified five versions of superstring theory, which were related by mathematical transformations called S-duality and T-duality. Attempts to connect M-theory to experiment focus on compactifying its extra dimensions, but none of the resulting models has been verified to produce the physics observed in high-energy experiments. According to Witten, the M could stand for "magic," "mystery," or "membrane."

American heavy metal band formed in 1981 by bassist Nikki Sixx and drummer Tommy Lee. The band has sold over 100 million records worldwide, and its 1989 album *Dr. Feelgood* was its only studio album to reach number one. A show planned as its final performance took place on New Year's Eve 2015, and the band announced its reunion in September 2018. In March 2019 it released four songs for the soundtrack of the [[Netflix]] biopic *The Dirt*. In 2022 it toured North America with [[Def Leppard]]. Guitarist Mick Mars retired from touring that October after 41 years, and John 5 replaced him.

Eastern Nilotic ethnic group native to Kenya and northern Tanzania. Their language, Maa, is related to Dinka, Kalenjin, and Nuer. The Maasai are [[Cattle|cattle]]-herding pastoralists with a reputation as fearsome warriors. Their territory reached its largest size in the mid-19th century, covering much of the Great Rift Valley. The period known as the Maasai "Emutai" (1883–1902) was marked by epidemics of rinderpest and smallpox, along with drought. Land was later taken for wildlife reserves and national parks, including the [[Ngorongoro Conservation Area]] and the [[Serengeti National Park|Serengeti]]. The Kenyan census reported 1,189,522 Maasai in 2019, compared with 377,089 in 1989. The Maasai have resisted government urging to adopt a sedentary lifestyle and have demanded grazing rights in national parks.

Proprietary [[Unix]] operating system developed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] for its [[Mac (computer)|Mac]] computers. Its first desktop version, Mac OS X 10.0, was released on March 24, 2001, succeeding the classic Mac OS. Its architecture came from NeXT's NeXTSTEP, which Apple acquired along with the return of [[Steve Jobs]]. Apple shortened the name to OS X in 2011 and changed it to macOS in 2016. As of April 2026, it was the second most widely used desktop operating system, after [[Microsoft Windows]] and ahead of all [[Linux]] distributions.

Brand of personal computers designed and marketed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] since 1984. The name is short for Macintosh, its official name until 1999. The original Macintosh launched in January 1984 at US$2,495, after Apple's "1984" advertisement during Super Bowl XVIII. Jef Raskin conceived the project in 1979, and [[Steve Jobs]] redefined it in 1981. Beginning in 1994 the line moved from Motorola 68000 processors to PowerPC, and it transitioned to Intel processors by 2006. Since 2020, Macs have used Apple silicon chips. They run [[MacOS|macOS]], which is not licensed to other manufacturers.

[[Genus]] of four species of trees in the [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]] family Proteaceae, indigenous to Australia. Native to northeastern [[New South Wales]] and central and southeastern [[Queensland]], the evergreen trees grow 2–12 m (7–40 ft) tall. Two species are commercially important for their nuts, which were first produced on a wide scale in Hawaii, where Australian seeds were introduced in the 1880s. Hawaii was the world's largest producer for more than a century, until South Africa took that position in the 2010s. Global production in 2025 was 344,000 metric tons (379,000 short tons). The macadamia is the only widely grown food plant native to Australia. The nuts of two other species contain cyanogenic glycosides.

Genus of 23 species of gregarious [[Old World monkey|Old World monkeys]], found throughout Asia, North Africa, and Europe (in Gibraltar). Macaques are principally frugivorous, although their diet also includes seeds, leaves, flowers, and tree bark. The long-tailed macaque (*M. fascicularis*) also eats small amounts of meat from shellfish, insects, and small mammals. All macaque social groups are arranged around dominant matriarchs. Aside from [[Human|humans]], macaques are the most widespread [[Primate|primate]] genus, ranging from Japan to the [[Indian subcontinent]] and, in the Barbary macaque, to North Africa and southern Europe. Some species have adapted to human settlements, and in urban areas of [[Southeast Asia]] they have become problematic because they can carry transmittable diseases. Their similarity to humans in emotional and cognitive development means they are often used in medical experiments. Most macaque species are listed as vulnerable to critically endangered on the IUCN Red List.

Special administrative region of [[China]] on the western side of the Pearl River estuary, consisting of the Macau Peninsula and the islands of Taipa and Coloane. The [[Ming dynasty]] first leased the territory to Portugal as a trading post in 1557, and it remained under Portuguese rule until the 1999 handover to China. It is governed under the principle of "one country, two systems," and its downtown architecture, blending Portuguese, French, English, Italian, and Chinese styles, was designated a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] in 2005. Macau is known for its [[Casino|casinos]], and its gambling industry is around seven times larger than that of [[Las Vegas]]. It is the most densely populated region in the world, and two-thirds of its total area is built on land reclaimed from the sea.

Tragedy by [[William Shakespeare]], first performed c. 1606. It is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, first published in the Folio of 1623, and it dramatizes the physically violent and psychological effects of political ambition. A Scottish general receives a prophecy from three witches that he will become king. Spurred by his wife, Lady Macbeth, he murders King Duncan and takes the throne. Racked with guilt and paranoia, he commits further murders and becomes a tyrannical ruler, and the couple's violence leads to their insanity and deaths. Shakespeare drew on the account in *Holinshed's Chronicles* (1587), though the events differ extensively from the history of the real Macbeth, a king of Scotland. Of Shakespeare's plays written during the reign of James I, it contains the most allusions to James, patron of Shakespeare's acting company. It has been adapted to film, television, [[Opera|opera]], and other media.

Ancient kingdom in the northeastern part of the Greek peninsula, later the dominant state of Hellenistic [[Greece]]. Centered at Aegae and later Pella, it was ruled by the Argead dynasty. Under Philip II (359–336 BC), Macedonia subdued mainland Greece and the Thracian [[Odrysian kingdom]], and it defeated Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC. His son, [[Alexander the Great]], overthrew the [[Achaemenid Empire]] and conquered territory as far as the [[Indus River]]. After Alexander's death in 323 BC, Macedonia remained a Greek cultural and political center. [[Aristotle]], Alexander's tutor, wrote works that became a keystone of Western philosophy. Macedonia's decline began with the rise of [[Rome]]. The monarchy was abolished in 168 BC, and after a short-lived revival in 150–148 BC, the Roman province of Macedonia was established.

Series of conflicts (214–148 BC) between the [[Roman Republic]] and several Greek kingdoms in the eastern Mediterranean. The wars comprised four conflicts with [[Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedonia]], one with the [[Seleucid Empire]], and a final minor war with the Achaean League. They gave Rome control or influence over Greece and the eastern Mediterranean, adding to its hegemony in the western Mediterranean after the Pyrrhic and [[Punic Wars]]. The First Macedonian War (214–205 BC) began when King Philip V allied himself with [[Hannibal]] during the Second Punic War; it ended indecisively with the Treaty of Phoenice. At Pydna in 168 BC, the Roman general Lucius Aemilius Paullus defeated the army of Perseus, abolishing the Macedonian monarchy. The Fourth Macedonian War (150–148 BC) ended with Macedonia becoming a Roman province, with its capital at Thessalonica.

Dimensionless quantity in [[Fluid dynamics|fluid dynamics]], the ratio of flow velocity past a boundary to the local speed of sound. It is named after Austrian physicist [[Ernst Mach]]. At Mach 1 the flow velocity equals the speed of sound; flow below Mach 1 is subsonic, and flow above it is supersonic. Compressibility effects are small when M is below 0.2–0.3 and the flow is quasi-steady and isothermal, allowing simplified incompressible flow equations. In dry air at mean [[Sea level|sea level]] and a standard temperature of 15 °C, the speed of sound is 340.3 meters per second.

Brazilian novelist, poet, playwright, and short-story writer, widely regarded as the greatest writer of Brazilian literature. Born in Rio de Janeiro, then capital of the [[Empire of Brazil]], to a poor family, he was the grandson of freed slaves. He barely attended public school and never attended university, and he became largely self-taught. He rose through newspapers and public positions. His work shaped the realist movement in Brazil, and he was known for his wit and critiques of society. His major works include *Dom Casmurro* (1899), *Quincas Borba*, and *Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas*. In 1897 he founded the Brazilian Academy of Letters and became its first president. He wrote over 200 short stories, and his story "A Missa do Galo" ("Midnight Mass," 1893) is often considered the greatest in Brazilian literature.

Broad, heavy blade originating in Central America, used as an agricultural implement similar to an axe or as a weapon. The Spanish word may be a diminutive of *macho*, a sledgehammer. The blade is typically 30 to 66 centimeters (12 to 26 in) long and usually under 3 millimeters (1⁄8 in) thick. In much of the English-speaking Caribbean the tool is called a cutlass. In Latin America it is used to cut [[Rainforest|rainforest]] undergrowth and sugar cane, and for household tasks such as splitting [[Coconut|coconuts]]. Many killings in the 1994 [[Rwandan genocide]] were carried out with machetes. In Cuba's independence wars, Máximo Gómez carried out the first [[Cavalry|cavalry]] charge using machetes as the primary weapon, on November 4, 1868. The machete is also a common side arm in West Africa, as in [[Chinua Achebe]]'s *Things Fall Apart*.

Fully automatic, rifled [[Firearm|firearm]] designed for sustained direct fire. Automatic weapons of 20 mm (0.79 in) caliber or more are usually classified as autocannons instead. Designed mainly as [[Infantry|infantry]] support weapons, machine guns are generally mounted on a bipod, tripod, or vehicle, and many use belt feeding. Unlike a semi-automatic firearm, it keeps firing for as long as the trigger is held. Machine guns are used against infantry, low-flying aircraft, small boats, and lightly armored vehicles. Heavy machine guns, between 12.7 mm (0.5 in) and 20 mm (0.8 in) in caliber, can be accurate at great distances. During the [[Vietnam War]], Carlos Hathcock set a long-distance record of 7,382 ft (2,250 m) with a .50 caliber heavy machine gun. The Model 1862 [[Gatling gun]], adopted by the United States Navy, was still powered by hand. Hiram Maxim later harnessed recoil energy to power reloading.

Field of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] concerned with statistical algorithms that learn from data and generalize to unseen data. [[Statistics|Statistics]] and mathematical optimization form its foundations. Arthur Samuel coined the term in 1959 while working at IBM, where he created a program that calculated the chances of winning at [[Checkers|checkers]]. In 1949 Donald Hebb proposed a theoretical neural structure that set the groundwork for many learning algorithms. Tom M. Mitchell's widely quoted definition holds that a computer program learns from experience with respect to some tasks if its performance at those tasks improves with experience. [[Deep learning|Deep learning]], which uses multilayered [[Neural network (machine learning)|neural networks]], has allowed these networks to surpass many earlier approaches. From the late 2000s and early 2010s, machine learning dominated AI, and the terms are often used interchangeably, though they are not synonymous.

Machine tool that changes the shape of a workpiece by applying pressure. Presses are classified by mechanism (hydraulic, mechanical, or pneumatic), by function (such as forging presses, stamping presses, press brakes, and punch presses), and by controllability, as conventional or servo presses. The most common frames are the C-frame, or gap-frame, and the straight-side press, which has vertical columns on either side and eliminates angular deflection. A press brake bends sheet metal and can apply bending forces of up to 3,000 tons. A shop press, typically applying between 1 and 30 tons, is used to press interference-fit parts together, such as gears onto shafts. A servo press, driven by an AC servo motor, consumes only 10–20% of the energy of other press machines. The steam hammer, first described by [[James Watt]] in 1784 but not built until 1840, began replacing manual and rotary-cam [[Hammer|hammers]] in the mid-19th century.
